architecture.name: turing-d256-perf-structure
architecture.head_dims: Performance structure of head_dim 256 (vs 128 baseline) attention on Turing sm_75 tensor cores, to ground an sm_75 bridge-kernel design decision. Precedent coverage examined: FA2-style monolithic d<=256, llama.cpp fattn-mma DKQ/DV in {64..576} including explicit Turing configs for (256,256), (320,256), (512,512), (576,512), and DefTruth's FFPA head-dim chunking at D=320..1024.
architecture.qkv_dim_divergence: The qk!=vo tuple view is well supported by the strongest precedent engine: llama.cpp fattn-mma instantiates asymmetric (DKQ=192,DV=128), (DKQ=320,DV=256) and (DKQ=576,DV=512) with per-arch Turing config rows, so a d-chunked pipeline does not require DKQ==DV (the K loop runs over DKQ/2 in nbatch_K2 chunks while the V tile is sized by nbatch_V2/DV). For the bridge target itself (Gemma-style symmetric d=256) qk==vo==256 is assumed symmetric.
architecture.kv_heads_gqa: GQA interacts with the d=256 budget only through query-column tiling: llama.cpp packs GQA partners into ncols=ncols1*ncols2 and on a Turing build forces total ncols=32 for all batch sizes ('Q->ne[1] <= 32/ncols2 || (NVIDIA && highest_compiled_arch == TURING)' -> ncols1=32/ncols2), i.e. Turing d=256 runs a 32-query-column x 64-KV-row tile with 4 warps regardless of GQA ratio; config rows exist for ncols=8/16/32/64.
architecture.hybrid_pattern: Not applicable to this item: all examined kernels (FA2, llama.cpp fattn-mma, FlashInfer FA2 prefill, FFPA) are standard softmax full-attention. Linear-attention/GDN kernels in llama.cpp (gated_delta_net.cu, gla.cu, wkv.cu) are separate op paths and impose no head-dim-256 constraint relevant here.
architecture.heterogeneous_dims: Per-layer divergence (e.g. Gemma-style 512-dim global layers) is out of sm_75 reach in every engine examined: llama.cpp fattn-mma does have Turing configs for (512,512) and (576,512) (decode-oriented, Q_in_reg=false, nbatch_fa=32, 4x128 DKQ chunking), which is the only verified code path that could serve 512-dim global layers on Turing; FlashInfer head_dim=512 is SM120/121-only and FA2 caps at 256 (Ampere+). [uncertain] No measured evidence that the llama.cpp Turing (512,512)/(576,512) configs are used in production models.

kernel_support.supported_dims: Three mechanisms documented. (1) FA2-style monolithic template: all head dims up to 256 via padding to multiples of 32 (flash-attn README: 'All head dimensions up to 256'), but the d=256 tile needs 96KB+ smem (see d256_feasibility) so on Turing the monolithic fwd path cannot launch; the local sm_75 patch (turing_lab/thirdparty/flash-attn, quilt/flash-attn-v2.8.3-sm75.patch, 'plan/0006') instantiates only small-tile splitKV kernels (kBlockM=64, kBlockN=128 for d<=64 else 64). (2) llama.cpp fattn-mma: native DKQ==DV==256 plus 320/256, 512/512, 576/512 via explicit per-arch config tables; on Turing the QK^T head dim is ALWAYS iterated in nbatch_K2=128-half2 (256-element) chunks with fp32 KQ_C accumulation - i.e. d=256 is structurally a 2x128 chained mma sequence, and d=512/576 is a 4x/4.5x chain. (3) FFPA (DefTruth/ffpa-attn-mma): MMA-level fine-grained tiling with constant 16-column head-dim slices, O(1) SRAM for any D. Instruction-level: Turing supports mma.m16n8k8.f16 (and m8n8k16 s8) but NOT m16n8k16 - llama.cpp mma.cuh: 'On Turing m16n8k16 mma is not available, use 2x m8n8k8 mma instead' (int8) and 2x/4x m16n8k8 for f16; the local FA2 patch likewise swaps MMA_Atom to SM75_16x8x8_F32F16F16F32_TN. ldmatrix (x2/x4/.trans) and movmatrix are available and used on Turing.
kernel_support.capability_gate: Real sm_75 constraints behind a d=256 kernel: (1) shared memory - Turing tuning guide: 'Shared memory capacity per SM is 64KB' and 'a single thread block can address the full 64 KB' (48KB static cap, opt-in above), with a 96KB unified L1/smem carved as 64+32 or 32+64; Ampere/Hopper have 100/164/228KB per block (SM86/89/80/90) which is why FA2's d=256 64x64 tile (96KB) is fine on A100/H100 and impossible on Turing. (2) Registers - 'The maximum registers per thread is 255', register file '64k 32-bit registers per SM' (Turing tuning guide); 32 warps/SM max. (3) No cp.async on sm_75: llama.cpp enables its multi-stage pipeline only when cp_async_available(cc) (sm_80+), so Turing fattn-mma runs nstages=0 synchronous loads and time-shares one K/V buffer. (4) mma shape gate: m16n8k16 requires sm_80; sm_75 tops out at m16n8k8 f16 - doubling instruction count for the same k-depth relative to Ampere atoms. None of these are soft 'CI gates': they are hard ISA/SM limits, unlike the FlashInfer-style host-side accounting bugs.
kernel_support.fallback_semantics: FA2-style kernels that exceed 64KB dynamic smem on Turing fail at cudaFuncSetAttribute(cudaFuncAttributeMaxDynamicSharedMemorySize) with 'invalid argument' at first launch (same failure class FlashInfer hit on sm_75 d=256 prefill before PR #3526 - see sibling research flashinfer-sm75-gap.json); FA2 upstream simply does not claim Turing ('please use FlashAttention 1.x for Turing GPUs', README). llama.cpp has no fallback needed for d=256 on Turing - fattn-mma is the selected kernel ('If Turing tensor cores are available, use them: return BEST_FATTN_KERNEL_MMA_F16'); unsupported head sizes (anything not in {40,64,72,80,96,112,128,192,256,320,512,576}) hard-abort ('GGML_ABORT("fatal error")') rather than pad. FFPA is a standalone research kernel with no dispatch layer.
kernel_support.ci_hardware_coverage: FA2: no Turing support claim, hence no sm_75 CI; the local sm_75 patch notes 'plan/0006' as an in-tree effort with no upstream CI. FlashInfer: no sm_75 attention CI (only a T4 sampling-only Jenkins stage; maintainer 'we don't have a SM75 CI machine' - verified in sibling research flashinfer-sm75-gap.json). llama.cpp: fattn-mma carries per-arch config tables for Turing/Volta/Ampere/CDNA/RDNA checked by static_asserts, and the project has a large community SM75+ user base, but [uncertain] whether llama.cpp CI exercises a real Turing GPU - no Turing runner was confirmed during this research; correctness for Turing fattn-mma is enforced by code review + community reports rather than a documented CI shard.

performance.turing_baseline: Quantitative Turing attention numbers are scarce and no d=256-vs-d=128 measured pair on the same Turing card was found anywhere. Verified data points: (1) FlashAttention-1 official T4 forward-only speedup plot (assets/flashattn_speedup_t4_fwd.jpg in the local tree): 2.3x-4.6x vs PyTorch standard attention across seqlen 128-2048 (speedup only; no TFLOPS printed; d=128-era kernel). (2) Peak ceilings from NVIDIA-documented rates: T4 = 65 FP16 TFLOPS (datasheet), which equals 40 SMs x 1.59GHz x 1024 FLOP/clk/SM; Turing whitepaper/blog: 'Eight Tensor Cores in an SM perform a total of 512 FP16 multiply and accumulate operations per clock, or 1024 total FP operations per clock', and the whitepaper spec tables list separate 'Peak FP16 Tensor TFLOPS with FP16 Accumulate' (2x) and 'with FP32 Accumulate' rows, i.e. FP16-accumulate runs at twice the FP32-accumulate rate. Derived peaks [derived, not directly quoted]: 2080 Ti (68 SM, ~1.545GHz) ~107.6 TFLOPS fp32-acc / ~215 fp16-acc; Quadro RTX 6000-class ~130 fp32-acc. (3) FFPA reported numbers are Ampere/Ada only (L20 d=512: 105 TFLOPS = 88% of 119 peak; RTX 4090: 149-191T; RTX 3080 Laptop: 25-44T; A30: 32-48T) with no Turing runs. [uncertain] No published achieved-TFLOPS figure for any attention kernel on T4/2080Ti exists to serve as a denominator; a local microbenchmark is required.
performance.d256_feasibility: Yes - but only with a chunked/time-shared design; a monolithic FA2-style d=256 tile does not fit Turing. Three independent proofs: (1) Shared memory: FA2 kSmemSize = kSmemQSize + kSmemKVSize with kSmemKVSize double-buffered: 64x64 tile at d=256 = 32,768 + 2*64*256*2 = 98,304B (96KB) > 64KB; even 64x32 = exactly 65,536B (in-tree comment '64 KB'), i.e. zero headroom, matching FlashInfer's post-#3526 FP16 d=256 sizeof(SharedStorageQKVO)=65536B exact-fit at NUM_MMA_KV=1. (2) llama.cpp solution: on Turing d=256 runs 128 threads (4 warps), nbatch_fa=64 KV rows, Q held in registers (Q_in_reg=true, freeing its smem tile - tile_K then starts at tile_Q), K and V time-multiplexing ONE buffer (tile_V aliases tile_K when nstages<=1, and Turing has no cp.async so nstages=0): a 64-row x 128-half2 tile = 32KB exactly with XOR swizzle (fattn-swizzle: stride=nbatch_2 when nbatch_2>=32 && %32==0, replacing the legacy +4-pad 264-half2 stride = 33.8KB decimal per buffer) plus ~4.6KB mask (32 rows x (64+8) x 2B) => ~36.6-38.4KB total, comfortably under 64KB. (3) Registers: an m16n8k8 chain holding O in fp32 needs D/8 x 4 registers per lane (32 x 4 = 128 at d=256 vs 16 x 4 = 64 at d=128) - concrete in FA2 terms: kBlockM x kHeadDim / kNThreads = 64*256/128 = 128 fp32 accumulator registers per thread before staging/softmax registers, against the 255/thread cap; llama.cpp halves this by keeping the VKQ accumulator in half2 (fp16 accumulation, T_C_VKQ half2 tile on Turing) giving ~64 registers, with fp32 accumulation retained only for KQ/S where softmax needs it, plus KQ_max/KQ_rowsum (cols_per_thread=2) and KQ_max_scale application per nbatch_fa block.
performance.cost_analysis: Quantified for the llama.cpp-style Turing d=256 design (the only one that ships): 4 warps/128 threads, tile 32 queries x 64 KV rows; per 64-row iteration QK^T = 32*64*256*2 = 1.05 MFLOP issued as m16n8k8 atoms: (32/16 rows-per-warp) x 32 cols... structurally 2 K-chunks x (nbatch_fa=64 rows / 16-row mma tiles) x (128 k / 8 k-per-mma) x 32 q-cols / 8 = 512 mma.m16n8k8.f32 per chunk-half, 1024 per full d=256 S; PV likewise 1024 mma (f16-acc) per iteration. At the documented 1024 FLOP/clk/SM (fp32-acc) rate an m16n8k8 f32-acc atom is 2 clk/SM (2048 FLOP), i.e. QK^T alone costs ~2048 SM-cycles per iteration per block - compute-bound at ~65 TFLOPS ceiling on T4 (65 TFLOPS / (65*2-45 overhead)) only if smem latency is hidden; Turing's synchronous (no cp.async) K/V loads with a single time-shared buffer mean K-load -> KQ-mma -> V-load -> PV-mma serialization, the main throughput risk vs Ampere double-buffering. Register budget: 128 fp32 (O, fp32 variant) or 64 half2 (llama.cpp variant) + Q_B fragments ~32 (32 cols x 256 half / 128 threads / 2 per reg... llama.cpp Q_B per-lane) + softmax state - designed to fit __launch_bounds__(128, 2) (<=128 regs/thread) [exact reg count not published]. Compile-time cost is documented: the FA2 sm_75 patch records 'The 256-wide kBlockN variants blow ptxas up (3.5+ h of 100% CPU without completing)', and even upstream FA2 notes large-tile variants spill ('block size (256 x 64) is 85% slower ... because of register spilling') - so d-chunked 16-wide-slice or 2x128 designs are also the compile-time-sane choice. FFPA's O(1)-SRAM 16-column slicing shows the chunking overhead can be near-zero on Ampere/Ada (1.8-3x vs SDPA); no Turing equivalent measured. [uncertain] exact ptxas register usage per design point.

design_fit.route: Route B (k-chunked 256 on the 128 pipeline) is the directly precedented design and this item's primary contribution: llama.cpp fattn-mma on Turing implements exactly 'S = QK^T accumulated over the k/head-dim dimension in two 128-deep m16n8k8 sequences with fp32 accumulation across chunks' (nbatch_K2=128 half2 per chunk, KQ_C fp32), DefTruth's FFPA (#1474/#1483) generalizes it to 16-column slices with O(1) SRAM in pure mma PTX, and FlashInfer/FA2 upstream cap out at exactly-fitting monolithic d=256 (FlashInfer NUM_MMA_KV=1, 65536B) or 512 on non-Turing archs. Route A (native d=256 template) is only viable at zero-headroom exact-fit and cannot double-buffer; Route C (unmodified FA2/FlashInfer headers) is blocked for d=256 prefill by the 64KB ceiling, not by headers.
design_fit.recommendation: For the sm_75 bridge kernel plan: adopt Route B with llama.cpp's exact Turing parameter set as the proven baseline - 128 threads (4 warps), 32 query columns, nbatch_fa=64 KV rows, Q in registers, one 64-row K/V smem tile time-multiplexed (32KB swizzled via fattn-swizzle-style XOR, or 33.8KB at the 264-half2 padded stride - the padded form leaves ~30KB slack for a second stage if cp.async-less prefetch is attempted), QK^T chunked 2x128 with fp32 S accumulation, softmax rescale per 64-row block, PV accumulated in fp16 (llama.cpp precedent) or fp32 only if ncols<=16 frees registers. Use m16n8k8 atoms (m16n8k16 does not exist on sm_75) and ldmatrix/movmatrix data movement. Next action: microbenchmark this shape on the local T4/2080 Ti at d=128 vs d=256 to fill the missing measured baseline, and decide fp16-vs-fp32 PV accumulation by comparing against the llama.cpp numerics envelope rather than inventing a stricter one.
design_fit.numerics_risks: Documented: (1) llama.cpp Turing path accumulates PV in fp16 (half2 VKQ_C) - precision loss over long sequences is accepted upstream, with per-64-row fp16 rescale by KQ_max_scale_h2 and an FTZ threshold (SOFTMAX_FTZ_THRESHOLD) zeroing vanishing scale factors; d=256 does not change this but doubles accumulated depth per output element vs d=128... actually PV accumulates over seqlen, unchanged by d; the d=256-specific risk is S accumulation order across the two 128-chunks (fp32, benign by matmul associativity, but changes bit-level results vs a monolithic d=256 GEMM). (2) Turing fragment permutations differ from Ampere: llama.cpp documents Turing-specific KQ_idx ((l/2)%2 or l%2 depending on tile width) and different shuffle offsets (offsets 2..1 vs Ampere's layout) - a port must replicate the Turing C-fragment layout, a classic wrong-output source. (3) No bf16 tensor-core mma on sm_75 (bf16 mma requires sm_80): d=256 Turing kernels are fp16-only, so bf16 models need an fp16 conversion wrapper. (4) tanhf-based logit softcap operates on fp32 KQ before exponentiation - safe. (5) FlashInfer's sm_75 d=256 exact-fit history (#3528: +48B broke launch for 6 weeks) shows the fragility of any zero-headroom (Route A) layout; chunked Route B with ~26KB slack is structurally more robust.
design_fit.demand_weighting: d=256 on Turing primarily serves Gemma-2/Gemma-3-family (head_dim 256) on the large T4/Colab and RTX 20-series installed base (sibling research head-dim-landscape/production-coverage items quantify model distribution; FlashInfer #1648: 'Tesla T4 and the RTX 20xx series are still the most common GPUs in the market'). The beneficiaries are inference providers on cheap T4 fleets and local users; vendor priority is low (no sm_75 attention CI anywhere examined; FA2 punted Turing to FA1; FlashInfer fixed d=256 sm_75 only after a user report). The existence of llama.cpp Turing configs for d=512/576 shows the same chunked machinery already extends to MLA-class shapes if DeepSeek-style demand materializes on Turing. [uncertain] share of Turing fleet actually serving d=256 models.
